 CHAPTER I 
       
 
1. BACKGROUND 
 
 Rule 204 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the 
Council of States (Rajya Sabha) provides that there  shall be a Committee on 
Subordinate Legislation to scrutinize and report to the Council whether the powers 
to make rules, regulations, bye-laws, schemes or ot her statutory instruments 
conferred by the Constitution or delegated by Parli ament have been properly 
exercised within such conferment or delegation, as the case may be.  
1.2. Mandate  
 Legislations passed by the Parliament and subseque ntly enacted after being 
assented to by the President of India, are implemen ted by the Executive i.e., 
various Ministries/Departments of Government of Ind ia. It is a well recognized 
principle that the laws enacted by Parliament canno t be exhaustive enough to 
visualize each and every situation that may arise d uring the course of its 
implementation and to make provisions for it in the  Act in anticipation. The 
Central Acts, therefore, if necessary,  contain a p rovision authorizing the 
Government to frame detailed rules/regulations, etc . to enable it to implement the 
provisions of the Act. These rules/regulations fram ed in exercise of the powers 
conferred by an Act of Parliament are termed as Subordinate Legislation.  
Rule 209 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of B usiness in the 
Council of States lays down that after each rule, r egulation, bye-law, scheme or 
other statutory instrument framed in pursuance of t he Constitution/Act or the 
legislative functions delegated by the Parliament t o a subordinate authority and 
which is required to be laid before Parliament, is so laid before the Council, the 
Committee shall, in particular consider: 
  
(i)  Whether the Order is in accord with the provis ions of the 
Constitution/Act pursuant to which it is made;  
(ii)  Whether the Order contains matter which, in t he opinion of the 
Committee, should more properly be dealt within an Act of Parliament;  
(iii) Whether the Order contains imposition of taxa tion;  
(iv)  Whether the Order directly or indirectly bars  the jurisdiction of the 
Courts; 
-1- 

(v)  Whether the Order gives retrospective effect t o any of the provisions in 
respect of which the Constitution or the Act does n ot expressly give any 
such power;  
(vi) Whether the Order involves expenditure from th e Consolidated Fund of 
India or the public revenues;  
(vii) Whether the Order appears to make some unusua l or unexpected use of 
the powers conferred by the Constitution or the Act  pursuant to which it 
is made;  
(viii) Whether there appears to have been unjustifi able delay in its publication 
or laying before Parliament; and 
(ix) Whether for any reason, the form or purport of  the order calls for any 
elucidation.  
 
1.3 Statutory Requirement for laying  
 
 The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya Sa bha had, in its 10 
th  
Report presented to the House on the 24 th  May, 1971, inter-alia  recommended, a 
standard laying formula to be incorporated not only  in new legislation but also in 
existing Acts as and when Bills to amend them are b rought before Parliament, 
which is reproduced below:- 
 “Every rule made by the Central Government under th is Act shall be laid, 
as soon as may be after it is made, before each Hou se of Parliament, while 
it is in session, for a total period of thirty days  which may be comprised in 
one session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry 
of the session immediately following the session or  the successive sessions 
aforesaid,  both Houses  agree in  making any modif ication to  the rule  or 
both Houses agree that the rule should not be made,  the rule shall 
thereafter have effect only in such modified form o r be of no effect, as the 
case may be; so, however, that any such modificatio n or annulment shall 
be without prejudice to the validity of anything pr eviously done under that 
rule.” 
 
Now, all statutes contain the above cited provision for making 
rules/regulations, for laying the same before both Houses of Parliament and right 
for amending or annulling the same.   
      
1.4 Time limit for laying of rules/regulations 
 
 As per the recommendations contained in para 33 of  the 1 
st  Report of the 
Committee, all the Orders including rules etc., are  required to be laid on the Table 
of the House: - 
(a)  within a period of 15 days after their publica tion in the Gazette, if the 
House is in session; and 
(b)  if the House is not in session, within a perio d of 15 days after the 
commencement  of  the  next  session. 
-2- 

 However, in case of notifications relating to a st ate under the President’s 
rule, due to difficulties faced by certain Ministry , the Committee vide its 
recommendations contained in its 6 th  Report (para 17-19) relaxed this time period 
to 30 days from the date of publication of the rules, orders, notifications etc., in the 
State Gazette. 
 
 
1.5 Motion for annulment or modification of rules/r egulations laid on the 
Table of the House 
 
 As per recommendations of the Committee contained in its 10
th  Report 
(cited at para 1.3 ante ), after the rules/regulations are laid on the Tabl e of the 
House, Members can move motion for modification or annulment of the 
rules/regulations. The statutory period of laying o f 30 days might be completed in 
one session or two or more successive sessions. Fur ther, as per the 
recommendation of the Committee contained in its 75 th  Report (Para 2.5), 
reproduced below:- 
 
"The Committee agrees with the view of the Committe e on Subordinate 
Legislation Lok Sabha (Seventh Lok Sabha) expressed  in its 20 
th  Report, that 
laying on the Table of all Orders' in pursuance of powers delegated by 
Parliament is very significant, as it affords an op portunity to Members of 
Parliament if they so desire to move any amendment or modification to such 
'order'; including a Motion for their annulment.”  
 Hence, a reading of both these recommendations tog ether indicates that 
Members have a right to suggest/move motion for ann ulment/modifications in the 
'Order' for a time period till one additional sessi on immediately following the 
session in which the period of 30 days is completed . If the modification or 
annulment is carried by the Houses of Parliament, t he rules/regulations stand 
annulled or modified to the extent agreed to by the Houses of Parliament. 
 
1.6 Role of the Committee on Subordinate Legislatio n, Rajya Sabha with 
regard to unjustifiable delay in laying 
 
 One of the important functions of the Committee, a ccording to Rule 209 
(viii), is to see whether there has been unjustifia ble delay in the publication or 
laying of the rules/regulations before the Parliame nt. The Committee monitors the 
laying of the rules/regulations etc. on the Table o f Rajya Sabha during its Session 
through its Reports. This practice started with the  131 
st  Report of the Committee 
on Statutory Orders laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha during its 190 th  Session, 
presented to the House on 15 th  December, 2000. During the meeting of the 
Committee held on 11 th  December, 2000, to adopt the said report, the Comm ittee 
decided that henceforth, it will regularly scrutini ze  the  notifications laid  on  the 
Table  of  Rajya Sabha from  
-3- 

time to time and present a report to the Council in  respect of each Session. This 
practice has continued since then and the present r eport is in pursuance of the said 
decision of the Committee.

Ministries/Departments have not put in good efforts  to obviate delay in 
placing these Notifications on the Table of Rajya S abha. The most

'inadvertently', 'delay in publication of Hindi ver sion', 'necessary 
administrative procedure of the Ministry', 'took time to collect the papers and 
complete the procedural formalities' etc. and none of the Ministries have cited 
any efforts made to overcome those administrative o bstacles  that delayed the 
laying of these Notification. Moreover, the failure  on the part of these 
Ministries to attach 'Delay Statements' to a majori ty of the delayed 
Notifications, which is an astonishing 62.20% of al l the delayed notifications, 
further indicates their lackadaisical attitude  tow ards their 
responsibility/scant regard to this august Committe e and   towards the 
Parliament.  
 The Committee expresses its displeasure to note th at among the 
Ministries that had multiple delayed Notifications,  Ministry of Corporate 
Affairs; Department of Financial Services and Minis try of Labour and

didn't. The Committee recommends that the following  Ministries which had

subordinate/attached offices/organizations, impressing upon them the

4. RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
 
a) Delay in Laying of Orders/Rules/Regulations 
 
  
4.1  The Committee notes that out of 82 delayed notific ations laid by the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India, duri ng the 250 
th  Session of 
Rajya Sabha. 2 Notifications were delayed by 4 mont h, 32 Notifications were 
delayed by 5 month; 7 by six months; 4 by seven mon ths; 1 by eight months; 
17 by nine months; and 19 by ten months  and above.  The Committee would 
like to single out few Ministries whose Notificatio ns were delayed by huge 
amount of time e.g., Department of Financial Services - 2 years and 7 months; 
Department of Revenue - 2 years and 5 months; and 3  years and 6 months; 
Department of Health and Family Welfare - 27 years and 5 months; 7 years 
and 3 months; and 11 years and 6 months. The Commit tee finds this utterly 
unacceptable and feels that delays for such long pe riods are beyond any logic. 
The Committee feels that this is in gross violation  of its recommendations 
contained in its 131 st  Report. The Committee in its 131 st  Report had 
recommended:- 
  
 “Orders required to be laid before the House shoul d be laid (i) if the 
House is not in Session, during the Session immedia tely following the date of 
publication of the Order in the Official Gazette an d (ii) if the House is in 
Session, on the date of the publication of the Orde r, during its continuance 
and in case the time lag between the date of public ation and the date of the 
closing of the Session is less than 15 clear days, before the expiry of the 
Session immediately following the said Session. All  the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India shoul d henceforth comply 
with this schedule in the matter of laying of the O rders issued under various 
Acts of Parliament on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.” 
 The Committee, while reiterating its above recomme ndations, 
recommends to the Ministries of Agriculture and Far mers Welfare 
(Department of Agriculture, Cooperation and Farmers  Welfare); 
 Civil 
Aviation; Commerce and Industry (Department of  Com merce) and 
(Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade); Corporate 
Affairs; Defence; Electronics and Information Techn ology; Finance 
(Department of Economic Affairs), (Department of Financial Services) and  

-22- 
(Department of Revenue); Health and Family Welfare  (Department of 
Health and Family Welfare); Home Affairs, Housing a nd Urban Affairs; 
Human Resource Development (Department of  Higher E ducation); Labour 
and Employment; Power; and Road Transport and Highw ays should ensure 
that all its notifications are laid on the Table of  Rajya Sabha within the

b) Non-attachment of ‘Delay Statements’to the delayed Notifications laid 
 
 
 
4.2  The most disconcerting point is that only 31 Notif ications out of total 
82 delayed Notifications that were laid during this  Session, had delay 
statements appended to them, which is mere 37.80% o f the total delayed 
Notifications. The Committee finds this totally una cceptable. The Committee, 
in its earlier recommendations contained in its 135 th  Report, reproduced 
below, had recommended that:- 
 
 “The Committee has, time and again, emphasized tha t it is essential that 
in case there is a delay in the laying of Statutory  Orders, the concerned 
Ministry/Department should invariably append a dela y statement along with 
the Notifications being laid so as to apprise the P arliament of the causes of 
delay. The Committee desires all Ministries/Departm ents to take a note of 
this, since the intention is that through the proce ss of formulation of a delay 
statement, the Ministry is able to introspect, iden tify bottlenecks and devise 
remedial measures”. 
 
 The Committee recommends that all the Ministries/D epartments must 
adhere to the time schedule for laying of Notificat ions as prescribed in 
Committee’s 131 
st  Report and append a delay statement in case there is  delay 
in laying. The delay statement gives an opportunity , to the Ministry to clarify 
the reasons for the delay in laying of the Notifica tion. In case this 
longstanding recommendations of the Committee is no t followed, then the 
accountability of the Ministries to the Parliament and the Constitutional 
Mandate of the Parliament to monitor the functionin g of the Executive would 
become a futile exercise and the Committee has ever y right to take this 
matter very seriously. 
 
c) Format of Delay Statements
 
 
4.3  The Committee further observes that even among the  few delay 
statements that were laid along with the Notificati ons, the reasons cited 
therein for the delay were very cryptic and unaccep table. None of the 
Ministries/Departments has made any sincere efforts  to identify the reasons 
for the delay in laying. They have cited reasons li ke "unavoidable 
circumstances", "unintentional", "inadvertently", "delay in    publication of  

-23- 
 
Hindi version", "necessary administrative procedure  of the Ministry", took 
time to collect the papers and complete the procedu ral formalities" etc. were 
submitted to the Highest Legislative Body in the Co untry. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministries/ Departments should cite 
cogent, logical and self explanatory reasons for th e delay in the laying of 
Notifications so that accountability of the Ministr ies/Departments to the 
Parliament is maintained  in its true letter and sp irit and to ensure that, it 
does remain a mere formality. In this connection, Committee would like to re-
iterate its recommendations contained in para 2(xii) of its 189 th  Report, which 
is reproduced below:- 
 
 “The Committee is not happy at the casual manner i n which the 
Ministries have treated its recommendations with re gard to the delay in the 
laying of the Notifications despite the Committee’s  reiteration in all its 
reports. The Committee is unable to accept the reas ons given by the 
Ministries for the delay in laying such as late rec eiving of printed copies of 
Notifications from the Government Press, administra tive reasons, time taken 
to complete procedural formalities, etc. The Commit tee takes serious note of 
the fact that, in most cases, the Ministries fail t o append delay statements 
explaining the reasons for the delay. Therefore, th e Committee reiterates, 
that the Ministries should take proactive measures so as to avoid any delay, 
whatsoever, in the laying of the Notifications and that the Committee is 
unable to accept the flimsy grounds given by the Mi nistries regarding the 
reasons for delay.” 
 
 The Committee, therefore, recommends these Ministr ies/Departments 
to not only ensure timely laying of Notifications b ut also follow the practice of 
enclosing a delay statement in case(s) of delays.

COMMITTEE ON SUBORDINATE  LEGISLATION, RAJYA SABHA  
 
4.4 The Committee in its earlier recommendations, f or strict compliance by all 
the Ministries/Departments of the Government of India, had stated that:- 
 
Formula for laying of Statutory Rules 
 
 The Committee approve the following draft revised f ormula for laying 
of Statutory Rules before both Houses of Parliament  which the Ministry of 
Law and Justice propose to incorporate in all future legislation which provide 
for making of rules by the Central Government:— 
 
 
 

-24- 
 "Every rule made by the Central Government under t his Act shall be 
laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before ea ch House of Parliament, 
while it is in session, for a total period of thirt y days which may be 
comprised in one session or in two or more successi ve sessions, and if, 
before the expiry of the session immediately follow ing the session or the 
successive sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in  making any 
modification in the rule or both Houses agree that the rule should not be 
made, the rule shall thereafter have effect only in  such modified form or 
be of no effect, as the case may be; so, however th at any such 
modification or annulment shall be without prejudic e to the validity of 
anything previously done under that rule." 
  
 The Committee recommends that the revised formula should be 
incorporated not only in new legislation but also i n the existing Acts as and 
when Bills to amend them are brought before Parliam ent. The Ministry 
should also incorporate the new formula in the Bill s pending before 
Parliament. This will, in the opinion of the Commit tee, bring about 
uniformity in the matter expeditiously.

does not find it possible to adhere to the time lim it, they should 
inform the Committee of the reasons why they cannot  make rules 
within the time limit and seek extension of time fo r completing the 
rule-making process.” 
(47 
th   Report) 
(Presented on 14 th  September, 1981) 
 
 
 “In addition to the concern expressed by the Commi ttee over delay in 
laying of Notifications on the Table of the House, the Committee also express 
their deep concern over delay in framing of rules/r egulations under different 
Acts. The Committee in its 47 
th  report presented to the House on 14.9.1981 
has recommended that the rule-making process should  be completed within a 
period of six months of the coming into force of an  Act. The Committee has 
further recommended that in case a Ministry is not able to adhere to this time 
limit, it should seek extension of time for complet ing the rule-making process. 
The recommendation of the committee reads as follows:- 
 
  “The Committee feels that the rule-making process  could 
well have been completed within the time limit of s ix months which 
the Committee has laid down for making of rules und er an Act after 
coming into force of that Act. Where however, a Min istry does not 
find it possible to adhere to the time limit, they should inform the 
Committee of the reasons why they cannot make rules  within the 
time limit and seek extension of time for completin g the rule-making 
process.” 

-26- 
 The Committee is constrained to take note of the f act that the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India are n ot complying with the 
Committee’s recommendation to complete the process of framing of 
subordinate legislation contemplated under various Acts of Parliament within 
a period of six months. At the same time, the Commi ttee also does not receive 
requests for extension of time for completing the r ule-making process in 
terms of its recommendations as above from most of the 
Ministries/Departments. The Committee takes a serious note of the prevailing 
situation in which the Ministries/Departments are n either able to complete 
the task of framing rules/regulations under differe nt Acts within the given six 
months’ period nor do they suo-motu  approach the Committee for seeking 
extension of time. The Committee further notes that  in order to ensure timely 
framing of rules/regulations it has taken an initia tive to monitor the progress 
of framing of subordinate legislation in respect of  all legislations brought 
about by different Ministries/Departments of Govern ment of India from the 
year 2003 onwards with a view to ensure that the fr aming of subordinate 
legislation is not delayed. The Committee, however,  finds that the responses 
from the Ministries/Departments have not been promp t in this monitoring 
exercise undertaken on behalf of the Committee. 
  
 In view of the above position, the Committee once again reiterates its 
recommendation that the Ministries/Departments shou ld ensure putting in 
place subordinate legislation positively within a p eriod of six months of 
coming into force of the Act. The Committee further recommends that in case 
the Ministry fails to meet with this deadline, they  should invariably approach 
the Committee for seeking extension of time. The Co mmittee further 
recommends that in cases where the time limit of si x months is not adhered 
to, they should, while laying rules/regulations bef ore the Parliament 
invariably lay a statement explaining the reasons w hy the framing of 
rules/regulations was delayed beyond six months so as to keep the Parliament 
apprised of the compliance of the Parliament’s mand ate  conferred upon the 
Executive.” 
 
(192 
nd 
 Report) 
(Presented on 26 th  August, 2011)  
 
The Committee observes that the whole process of en acting laws is 
defeated if rules are not framed and laid on the Table of the House in time.  A 
reasonable delay could be understood but unjustifia bly long delays should be 
avoided and the Ministries should work towards improving this position.   The 
Committee hopes that Ministry would strive to keep the delay to the 
minimum and take care that Notifications are laid o n the Table of the House 
at the first available opportunity after publication of Notifications. 
 
 
 

-27- 
The Committee would like to impress upon the Minist ry that it is their 
responsibility to ensure that copies of the Notific ations are printed timely and 
for this purpose, they need to evolve a suitable me chanism to ensure that 
notifications are laid in time.   The Committee is happy that the Ministry has 
evolved an internal mechanism/ procedure for this p urpose.  The Committee 
hopes that it would take action accordingly in orde r to comply with the 
prescribed schedule in the matter of laying of statutory Notifications. 
 
The Ministry must take appropriate step to remove l acuna, if any, 
administrative or otherwise, causing such long dela y by being little proactive 
and prompt.  Further, the Ministries should take it  up with the Ministry of 
Urban Development for late receiving of printed copies of the Notification. 
212 
th  Report 
(Presented on 3 rd  September, 2013) 
 
 
 
Planning to lay papers during the initial stages of the Session 
 
 
 "The Committee recommends that Ministries should pl an to lay their 
papers during the initial/middle stages of the sess ion rather than scheduling 
this work towards the close of the session in order to avoid such happenings." 
 
173 
rd   Report 
(Presented on 22 nd  April, 2008) 
 
Uploading Notifications on websites 
 
 
  Rules/Regulations/Orders/bye-laws are laid by dif ferent Ministries on 
the Table of the House under various provisions of parent Acts passed by 
Parliament. These Rules/ Regulations/Orders/bye-law s are published in the 
official Gazette before being laid on the Table of the House. Even after they 
are laid, it is very difficult to get access to the se Notifications. The Committee 
recommends that such Rules/Regulations/Orders, etc. laid on the Table of the 
House should be invariably uploaded on the websites  of respective Ministries 
immediately on the same day when they have been lai d on the Table of the 
House, for information of Members of Parliament and  people at large for 
their easy access. 
 
201 
st  Report 
(Presented on 14 th  December, 2012)  
 
 
 
 
 

-28- 
Late availability of printed copies  
 
 “The Committee is not inclined to accept the late availability of 
printed copies of Notifications from the Government  of India Press as the 
reason for delay in laying of the Notifications. Th e Committee directs all the 
Ministries that in case there is a delay in procuri ng printed copies in time, 
they may obtain G.S.R. and S.O. numbers from the Go vernment of India 
Press and prepare requisite number of copies in cyclostyled form for laying in 
the Parliament. The Committee also recommends that this process may be 
adopted by Ministries suo moto  on immediate basis so as to avoid such delays 
henceforth”. 
213 
th  Report 
(Presented on 19 th  February, 2014) 
 
 The Committee recommends that all the Ministries/De partments 
should follow the above recommendations meticulously.

CHAPTER I  
      
1.         BACKGROUND  
  
            Rule 204 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of 
States (Rajya Sabha) provides that there shall be a  Committee on Subordinate 
Legislation to scrutinize and report to the Council  whether the powers to make rules, 
regulations, bye-laws, schemes or other statutory i nstruments conferred by the 
Constitution or delegated by Parliament have been p roperly exercised within such 
conferment or delegation, as the case may be. 
1.2.      Mandate  
            Legislations passed by the Parliament a nd subsequently enacted after being 
assented to by the President of India, are implemen ted by the Executive i.e., various 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India. It i s a well recognized principle that 
the laws enacted by Parliament cannot be exhaustive  enough to visualize each and 
every situation that may arise during the course of  its implementation and to make 
provisions for it in the Act in anticipation. The C entral Acts, therefore, if 
necessary,  contain a provision authorizing the Gov ernment to frame detailed 
rules/regulations, etc. to enable it to implement t he provisions of the Act. These 
rules/regulations framed in exercise of the powers conferred by an Act of Parliament 
are termed as Subordinate Legislation. 
Rule 209 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of B usiness in the Council of 
States lays down that after each rule, regulation, bye-law, scheme or other statutory 
instrument framed in pursuance of the Constitution/ Act or the legislative functions 
delegated by the Parliament to a subordinate authority and which is required to be laid 
before Parliament, is so laid before the Council, t he Committee shall, in particular 
consider: 
  
(i) Whether the Order is in accord with the provisions of the       
Constitution/Act  pursuant to which it is made; 
(ii) Whether the Order contains matter which, in the opi nion of the 
Committee, should more properly be dealt within an Act of Parliament; 
(iii) Whether the Order contains imposition of taxation; 
(iv) Whether the Order directly or indirectly bars the j urisdiction of the 
Courts; 
(v) Whether the Order gives retrospective effect to any of the provisions in 
respect of which the Constitution or the Act does n ot expressly give 
any such power; 
(vi) Whether the Order involves expenditure from the Con solidated Fund 
of India or the public revenues; 

6 
 
(vii)     Whether the Order appears to make some unusual or unexpected use of 
the powers conferred by the Constitution or the Act  pursuant to which 
it is made; 
(viii)    Whether there appears to have been unjust ifiable delay in its 
publication or laying before Parliament; and 
 
(ix)      Whether for any reason, the form or purpo rt of the order calls for any 
elucidation. 
  
1.3       Statutory Requirement for laying  
  
            The Committee on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya Sabha had, in its 10 
th Report 
presented to the House on the 24 th  May, 1971, inter-alia  recommended, a standard 
laying formula to be incorporated not only in new l egislation but also in existing Acts 
as and when Bills to amend them are brought before Parliament, which is reproduced 
below:- 
 “Every rule made by the Central Government under th is Act shall be laid, as 
soon as may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament, while it is in 
session, for a total period of thirty days which ma y be comprised in one 
session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the 
session immediately following the session or the su ccessive sessions 
aforesaid,  both Houses  agree in  making any modif ication to  the rule  or 
both Houses agree that the rule should not be made,  the rule shall thereafter 
have effect only in such modified form or be of no effect, as the case may be; 
so, however, that any such modification or annulmen t shall be without 
prejudice to the validity of anything previously done under that rule.”  
  
Now, all statutes contain the above cited provision for making 
rules/regulations, for laying the same before both Houses of Parliament and right for 
amending or annulling the same.  
                                                            
1.4       Time limit for laying of rules/regulations  
  
            As per the recommendations contained in  para 33 of the 1 
st  Report of the 
Committee, all the Orders including rules etc., are  required to be laid on the Table of 
the House: - 
(a)  within a period of 15 days after their publica tion in the Gazette, if the 
House is in session; and 
(b)  if the House is not in session, within a perio d of 15 days after the 
commencement  of  the  next  session. 
 
            However, in case of notifications relat ing to a state under the President’s rule, 
due to difficulties faced by certain Ministry, the Committee vide its recommendations 
contained in its 6 
th  Report (para 17-19) relaxed this time period to 30  days from the 
date of publication of the rules, orders, notifications etc., in the State Gazette. 
  
 
 
 

7 
 
 1.5       Motion for annulment or modification of r ules/regulations laid on the 
Table of the House  
  
            As per recommendations of the Committee  contained in its 10 
th  Report 
(cited at para 1.3 ante ), after the rules/regulations are laid on the Tabl e of the House, 
Members can move motion for modification or annulme nt of the rules/regulations. 
The statutory period of laying of 30 days might be completed in one session or two or 
more successive sessions. Further, as per the recom mendation of the Committee 
contained in its 75 th  Report (Para 2.5), reproduced below:- 
  
"The Committee agrees with the view of the Committe e on Subordinate 
Legislation Lok Sabha (Seventh Lok Sabha) expressed  in its 20 th  Report, that 
laying on the Table of all Orders' in pursuance of powers delegated by 
Parliament is very significant, as it affords an op portunity to Members of 
Parliament if they so desire to move any amendment or modification to such 
'order'; including a Motion for their annulment.”  
            Hence, a reading of both these recommen dations together indicates that 
Members have a right to suggest/move motion for ann ulment/modifications in the 
'Order' for a time period till one additional sessi on immediately following the session 
in which the period of 30 days is completed. If the  modification or annulment is 
carried by the Houses of Parliament, the rules/regu lations stand annulled or modified 
to the extent agreed to by the Houses of Parliament. 
  
1.6       Role of the Committee on Subordinate Legi slation, Rajya Sabha with 
regard to unjustifiable delay in laying  
  
            One of the important functions of the Committee, according to Rule 209 (viii), 
is to see whether there has been unjustifiable dela y in the publication or laying of the 
rules/regulations before the Parliament. The Commit tee monitors the laying of the 
rules/regulations etc. on the Table of Rajya Sabha during its Session through its 
Reports. This practice started with the 131 
st  Report of the Committee on Statutory 
Orders laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha during its 190 th  Session, presented to the 
House on 15 th  December, 2000. During the meeting of the Committe e held on 
11 th   December,    2000,  to  adopt  the   said  report ,  the    Committee  decided    that 
henceforth, it will regularly scrutinize  the  noti fications laid  on  the Table  of  Rajya 
Sabha fromtime to time and present a report to the Council in respect of each Session. 
This practice has continued since then and the pres ent report is in pursuance of the 
said decision of the Committee.

            The Committee observes that 11 Notifica tions, which account for  22.91% 
of all the delayed Notifications, were late by 10 o r more months; 2 Notifications, 
which comes to 4.17% of all the delayed Notificatio ns, were late by 7 months; 1 
Notification which comes to 2.08% of all the delaye d Notifications was late by 6 
months; 8 Notifications, which comes to 16.7% of al l the delayed Notifications, 
were late by 5 months;  12 Notifications, which com es to 25% of all the delayed 
Notifications were late by 4 months; and 14 Notific ations, which come to 29.17% 
of all the delayed Notifications were late by 3 mon ths. This shows that some of 
the Ministries/Departments have not put in good eff orts to obviate delay in 
placing these Notifications on the Table of Rajya S abha. The most disappointing 
fact was that none of the  Ministries/Departments h as made any sincere effort to 
identify the logical reasons for the delay in layin g. They have cited reasons like 
"limited business days"; "primary focus on other ma tters"; "administrative 
difficulty";  "inadvertent delay due to administrat ive reasons"; "due to 
oversight, which is regretted" etc. and none of the  Ministries have cited any 
efforts made to overcome those administrative obsta cles  that delayed the laying 
of these Notification. Moreover, the failure on the  part of these Ministries to 
attach 'Delay Statements' to a majority of the dela yed Notifications, (i.e. 31 
Notifications), which is an astonishing 64.58% of a ll the delayed notifications, 
further indicates their lackadaisical attitude  tow ards their responsibility/scant 
regard to this august Committee and   towards the Parliament.  
            The Committee expresses its displeasure  to note that among the 
Ministries that had multiple delayed Notifications,  Ministry of Civil Aviation; 
Consumer  Affairs, Food and Public Distribution (De partment of Consumer 
Affairs); Ministry of  Power; and Ministry of Texti les had attached 'Delay 
Statements' to all their delayed Notifications;  wh ile Ministry of Finance 
(Department of Revenue); and Ministry of Home Affai rs had attached Delay 
Statements to some of their delayed Notifications. The Committee also observe 
that the Ministries of Agriculture and Farmers Welf are (Department of 
Agriculture, Research and Education); Corporate Aff airs; Finance (Department 
of  Economic Affairs) and (Department of Financial Services); Housing and 
Urban Affairs; Human Resource Development (Departme nt of Higher 
Education); Mines; Road Transport and Highways; and  Shipping, did not even 
bother to attach 'Delay Statement' giving reasons f or the delay in laying their 
Notifications on the Table of Rajya Sabha. The Comm ittee recommends that the 
following Ministries which had multiple delayed Not ifications, like, Ministries of 
Agriculture and Farmers Welfare (Department of Agri culture, Research and 
Education); Civil Aviation; Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution 
(Department of Consumer Affairs); Corporate Affairs ; Finance (Department 
of  Economic Affairs); (Department of Financial Ser vices) and (Department of 
Revenue); Home Affairs; Housing and Urban Affairs; Human Resource 
Development (Department of Higher Education); Mines ; Power; Road 
Transport and Highways; Shipping and Textiles; issu e instructions to all its 
Departments and their subordinate/attached offices/ organizations, impressing 
upon them the importance of laying all notification s within the stipulated time 
and if there is any delay, then to attach a delay s tatement, explaining the cogent 

19 
 
reasons for the delay and the steps taken to obviat e such reasons in future. The 
Committee also recommends that following recommenda tions of the Committee 
on Subordinate Legislation, Rajya Sabha should be c irculated to all the 
Ministries/Departments for strict compliance. The M inistry of Parliamentary 
Affairs may take necessary steps to co-ordinate wit h other 
Ministries/Departments on this serious issue.  
            
  
4.         RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  
a) Delay in Laying of Orders/Rules/Regulations  
            
4.1    The Committee notes that out of 48 delayed notif ications laid by the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India, duri ng the 251 st  Session of 
Rajya Sabha, 14 Notifications were delayed by 3 mon ths; 12 Notifications were 
delayed by 4 months; 8 by five months; 1 by six mon ths; 2 by seven months; and 
11 by ten months or more. The Committee would like to single out few Ministries 
whose Notifications were delayed by huge amount of time e.g., Agriculture and 
Farmers Welfare (Department of Agriculture, Researc h and Education)  - 1 
year; and 1 year and 6 months; Civil Aviation - 1 y ear and 5 months; 1 year and 
4 months; and 1 year and 5 months; Home Affairs - 2  years and 10 months; and 
1 year and 1 month; Power - 1 year and 1 month; and  11 months. The 
Committee finds this utterly unacceptable and feels  that delays for such long 
periods are beyond any logic. The Committee feels t hat this is in gross violation 
of the recommendations contained in its 131 st  Report. The Committee in its 
131 st  Report had recommended:- 
            
        “Orders required to be laid before the Hous e should be laid (i) if the House 
is not in Session, during the Session immediately f ollowing the date of 
publication of the Order in the Official Gazette an d (ii) if the House is in Session, 
on the date of the publication of the Order, during  its continuance and in case 
the time lag between the date of publication and th e date of the closing of the 
Session is less than 15 clear days, before the expi ry of the Session immediately 
following the said Session. All the Ministries/Depa rtments of Government of 
India should henceforth comply with this schedule i n the matter of laying of the 
Orders issued under various Acts of Parliament on t he Table of the Rajya 
Sabha.”  
            The Committee, while reiterating its ab ove recommendations, 
recommends to the Ministries of Agriculture and Far mers Welfare (Department 
of Agriculture, Research and Education) Civil Aviation; Consumer Affairs, Food 
and Public Distribution (Department of Consumer Aff airs); Corporate Affairs; 
Finance (Department of  Economic Affairs); (Departm ent of Financial Services) 
and (Department of Revenue); Home Affairs; Housing and Urban Affairs; 
Human Resource Development (Department of Higher Ed ucation); Mines; 
Power; Road Transport and Highways; Shipping and Textiles should ensure that 
all its notifications are laid on the Table of Rajy a Sabha within the prescribed 
time of 15 days.  
  
 
 

20 
 
b) Non-attachment of ‘Delay Statements’to the delayed Notifications laid  
  
4.2        The most disconcerting point is that only 17  Notifications out of total 48 
delayed Notifications that were laid during this Se ssion, had delay statements 
appended to them, which is mere 35.42% of the total  delayed Notifications. The 
Committee finds this totally unacceptable. The Comm ittee, in its earlier 
recommendations contained in its 135th Report, repr oduced below, had 
recommended that:- 
  
        “The Committee has, time and again, emphasi zed that it is essential that in 
case there is a delay in the laying of Statutory Or ders, the concerned 
Ministry/Department should invariably append a dela y statement along with the 
Notifications being laid so as to apprise the Parli ament of the causes of delay. 
The Committee desires all Ministries/Departments to  take a note of this, since 
the intention is that through the process of formul ation of a delay statement, the 
Ministry is able to introspect, identify bottleneck s and devise remedial 
measures”.  
  
            The Committee recommends that all the M inistries/Departments must 
adhere to the time schedule for laying of Notificat ions as prescribed in its 
131 st  Report and append a delay statement in case there is  delay in laying. The 
delay statement gives an opportunity to the Ministr y to clarify the reasons for 
the delay in laying of the Notification. In case th is longstanding recommendation 
of the Committee is not followed, then the accounta bility of the Ministries to the 
Parliament and the Constitutional Mandate of the Pa rliament to monitor the 
functioning of the Executive would become a futile exercise and the Committee 
has every right to take this matter very seriously. 
  
c) Format of Delay Statements  
  
4.3        The Committee further observes that even amo ng the few delay 
statements that were laid along with the Notificati ons, the reasons cited therein 
for the delay were very cryptic and unacceptable. N one of the 
Ministries/Departments has made any sincere efforts  to identify the reasons for 
the delay in laying. They have cited reasons like " limited business days"; 
"primary focus on other matters"; "administrative d ifficulty";  "inadvertent 
delay due to administrative reasons"; "due to overs ight, which is regretted" 
were submitted to the Highest Legislative Body of t he Country. The Committee, 
therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministries/ Departments should cite 
cogent, logical and self explanatory reasons for th e delay in the laying of 
Notifications so that accountability of the Ministr ies/Departments to the 
Parliament is maintained  in its true letter and sp irit and to ensure that, it does 
remain a mere formality. In this connection, Commit tee would like to re-iterate 
its recommendations contained in para 2(xii) of its 189 th  Report, which is 
reproduced below:- 
  
             “The Committee is not happy at the cas ual manner in which the 
Ministries have treated its recommendations with re gard to the delay in the 
laying of the Notifications despite the Committee’s  reiteration in all its reports. 
The Committee is unable to accept the reasons given  by the Ministries for the 

21 
 
delay in laying such as late receiving of printed c opies of Notifications from the 
Government Press, administrative reasons, time take n to complete procedural 
formalities, limited business days, etc. The Commit tee takes serious note of the 
fact that, in most cases, the Ministries fail to ap pend delay statements explaining 
the reasons for the delay. Therefore, the Committee  reiterates, that the 
Ministries should take proactive measures so as to avoid any delay, whatsoever, 
in the laying of the Notifications and that the Com mittee is unable to accept the 
flimsy grounds given by the Ministries regarding the reasons for delay.”  
  
            The Committee, therefore, recommends th ese Ministries/Departments to 
not only ensure timely laying of Notifications but also follow the practice of 
enclosing a delay statement in case(s) of delays.  
  
  
  

22 
 
d) EARLIER IMPORTANT RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
ON SUBORDINATE  LEGISLATION, RAJYA SABHA  
  
4.4       The Committee in its earlier recommendati ons, for strict compliance by all the 
Ministries/Departments of the Government of India, had stated that:- 
  
Formula for laying of Statutory Rules 
 
  
            The Committee approve the following draft revised f ormula for laying of 
Statutory Rules before both Houses of Parliament wh ich the Ministry of Law 
and Justice propose to incorporate in all future le gislation which provide for 
making of rules by the Central Government:— 
  
        "Every rule made by the Central Government under this Act shall be 
laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before ea ch House of Parliament, 
while it is in session, for a total period of thirt y days which may be 
comprised in one session or in two or more successi ve sessions, and if, before 
the expiry of the session immediately following the  session or the successive 
sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any  modification in the rule 
or both Houses agree that the rule should not be ma de, the rule shall 
thereafter have effect only in such modified form o r be of no effect, as the 
case may be; so, however that any such modification  or annulment shall be 
without prejudice to the validity of anything previ ously done under that 
rule."  
            
            The Committee recommends that the revis ed formula should be 
incorporated not only in new legislation but also i n the existing Acts as and when 
Bills to amend them are brought before Parliament. The Ministry should also 
incorporate the new formula in the Bills pending be fore Parliament. This will, in 
the opinion of the Committee, bring about uniformit y in the matter 
expeditiously.

Time limit for rule making process

................. Where however, a Ministry does no t find it possible to adhere to the

            “In addition to the concern expressed b y the Committee over delay in

recommendation of the committee reads as follows:- 
  
               “The Committee feels that the rule-m aking process could well have

down for making of rules under an Act after coming into force of that Act. 
Where however, a Ministry does not find it possible  to adhere to the time limit,

24 
 
            
            The Committee is constrained to take no te of the fact that the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India are n ot complying with the 
Committee’s recommendation to complete the process of framing of subordinate 
legislation contemplated under various Acts of Parl iament within a period of six 
months. At the same time, the Committee also does n ot receive requests for 
extension of time for completing the rule-making pr ocess in terms of its 
recommendations as above from most of the Ministrie s/Departments. The 
Committee takes a serious note of the prevailing si tuation in which the 
Ministries/Departments are neither able to complete  the task of framing 
rules/regulations under different Acts within the given six months’ period nor do 
they suo-motu  approach the Committee for seeking extension of ti me. The 
Committee further notes that in order to ensure tim ely framing of 
rules/regulations it has taken an initiative to mon itor the progress of framing of 
subordinate legislation in respect of all legislati ons brought about by different 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India from the year 2003 onwards 
with a view to ensure that the framing of subordina te legislation is not delayed. 
The Committee, however, finds that the responses fr om the 
Ministries/Departments have not been prompt in this  monitoring exercise 
undertaken on behalf of the Committee.  
  
            In view of the above position, the Comm ittee once again reiterates its 
recommendation that the Ministries/Departments shou ld ensure putting in place 
subordinate legislation positively within a period of six months of coming into 
force of the Act. The Committee further recommends that in case the Ministry 
fails to meet with this deadline, they should invar iably approach the Committee 
for seeking extension of time. The Committee furthe r recommends that in cases 
where the time limit of six months is not adhered t o, they should, while laying 
rules/regulations before the Parliament invariably lay a statement explaining the 
reasons why the framing of rules/regulations was de layed beyond six months so 
as to keep the Parliament apprised of the complianc e of the Parliament’s 
mandate  conferred upon the Executive.”  
(192 nd  Report)  
(Presented on 26 th  August, 2011)  
  
The Committee observes that the whole process of en acting laws is 
defeated if rules are not framed and laid on the Ta ble of the House in time.  A 
reasonable delay could be understood but unjustifia bly long delays should be 
avoided and the Ministries should work towards impr oving this position.   The 
Committee hopes that Ministry would strive to keep the delay to the minimum 
and take care that Notifications are laid on the Ta ble of the House at the first 
available opportunity after publication of Notifications.  
  
The Committee would like to impress upon the Minist ry that it is their 
responsibility to ensure that copies of the Notifications are printed timely and for 
this purpose, they need to evolve a suitable mechan ism to ensure that 
notifications are laid in time.   The Committee is happy that the Ministry has 
evolved an internal mechanism/ procedure for this p urpose.  The Committee 
hopes that it would take action accordingly in orde r to comply with the 
prescribed schedule in the matter of laying of statutory Notifications.  

25 
 
  
The Ministry must take appropriate step to remove l acuna, if any, 
administrative or otherwise, causing such long delay by being little proactive and 
prompt.  Further, the Ministries should take it up with the Ministry of Urban 
Development for late receiving of printed copies of the Notification.  
212 th  Report  
(Presented on 3 rd  September, 2013)  
  
  
Planning to lay papers during the initial stages of the Session  
  
        "The Committee recommends that Ministries should pl an to lay their 
papers during the initial/middle stages of the sess ion rather than scheduling this 
work towards the close of the session in order to avoid such happenings."  
  
173 
rd   Report  
(Presented on 22 nd  April, 2008)  
  
Uploading Notifications on websites 
 
  
            Rules/Regulations/Orders/bye-laws are l aid by different Ministries on the 
Table of the House under various provisions of pare nt Acts passed by 
Parliament. These Rules/ Regulations/Orders/bye-law s are published in the 
official Gazette before being laid on the Table of the House. Even after they are 
laid, it is very difficult to get access to these N otifications. The Committee 
recommends that such Rules/Regulations/Orders, etc.  laid on the Table of the 
House should be invariably uploaded on the websites  of respective Ministries 
immediately on the same day when they have been lai d on the Table of the 
House, for information of Members of Parliament and  people at large for their 
easy access.  
  
201 st  Report  
(Presented on 14 th  December, 2012)  
  
   
Late availability of printed copies  
  
            “The Committee is not inclined to accep t the late availability of printed 
copies of Notifications from the Government of Indi a Press as the reason for 
delay in laying of the Notifications. The Committee  directs all the Ministries that 
in case there is a delay in procuring printed copie s in time, they may obtain 
G.S.R. and S.O. numbers from the Government of Indi a Press and prepare 
requisite number of copies in cyclostyled form for laying in the Parliament. The 
Committee also recommends that this process may be adopted by Ministries suo 
moto  on immediate basis so as to avoid such delays henceforth”.  
213 
th  Report  
(Presented on 19 th  February, 2014)  
  
            The Committee recommends that all the Ministries/De partments should 
follow the above recommendations meticulously.

              REPORT           
  CHAPTER I  
1.         BACKGROUND  
      Rule 204 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduc t of Business in the Council of 
States (Rajya Sabha) provides that there shall be a  Committee on Subordinate 
Legislation to scrutinize and report to the Council  whether the powers to make rules, 
regulations, bye-laws, schemes or other statutory i nstruments conferred by the 
Constitution or delegated by Parliament have been p roperly exercised within such 
conferment or delegation, as the case may be. 
1.2.      Mandate  
            Legislations passed by the Parliament a nd subsequently enacted after being 
assented to by the President of India, are implemen ted by the Executive i.e., various 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India. It i s a well recognized principle that 
the laws enacted by Parliament cannot be exhaustive  enough to visualize each and 
every situation that may arise during the course of  its implementation and to make 
provisions for it in the Act in anticipation. The C entral Acts, therefore, if 
necessary,  contain a provision authorizing the Gov ernment to frame detailed 
rules/regulations, etc. to enable it to implement t he provisions of the Act. These 
rules/regulations framed in exercise of the powers conferred by an Act of Parliament 
are termed as Subordinate Legislation. 
Rule 209 of the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of B usiness in the Council of 
States lays down that after each rule, regulation, bye-law, scheme or other statutory 
instrument framed in pursuance of the Constitution/ Act or the legislative functions 
delegated by the Parliament to a subordinate author ity and which is required to be laid 
before Parliament, is so laid before the Council, t he Committee shall, in particular 
consider: 
  
(i)         Whether the Order is in accord with the  provisions of the 
Constitution/Act pursuant to which it is made; 
(ii)        Whether the Order contains matter which , in the opinion of the 
Committee, should more properly be dealt within an Act of Parliament; 
(iii)       Whether the Order contains imposition of taxation; 
(iv)       Whether the Order directly or indirectly  bars the jurisdiction of the 
Courts; 
-1- 

(v)        Whether the Order gives retrospective ef fect to any of the provisions 
in respect of which the Constitution or the Act doe s not expressly give any 
such power; 
(vi)       Whether the Order involves expenditure f rom the Consolidated Fund 
of India or the public revenues; 
(vii)      Whether the Order appears to make some u nusual or unexpected use 
of the powers conferred by the Constitution or the Act pursuant to which it is 
made; 
(viii)     Whether there appears to have been unjus tifiable delay in its 
publication or laying before Parliament; and 
(ix)       Whether for any reason, the form or purport of the order calls for any 
elucidation. 
 1.3       Statutory Requirement for laying  
             The Committee on Subordinate Legislati on, Rajya Sabha had, in its 10 
th  
Report presented to the House on the 24 th  May, 1971, inter-alia  recommended, a 
standard laying formula to be incorporated not only  in new legislation but also in 
existing Acts as and when Bills to amend them are b rought before Parliament, which 
is reproduced below:- 
 “Every rule made by the Central Government under th is Act shall be laid, as 
soon as may be after it is made, before each House of Parliament, while it is in 
session, for a total period of thirty days which ma y be comprised in one 
session or in two or more successive sessions, and if, before the expiry of the 
session immediately following the session or the su ccessive sessions 
aforesaid,  both Houses  agree in  making any modification to  the rule  or both 
Houses agree that the rule should not be made, the rule shall thereafter have 
effect only in such modified form or be of no effec t, as the case may be; so, 
however, that any such modification or annulment sh all be without prejudice 
to the validity of anything previously done under that rule.”  
  Now, all statutes contain the above cited provision for making 
rules/regulations, for laying the same before both Houses of Parliament and for 
amending or annulling the same.  
1.4       Time limit for laying of rules/regulations  
             As per the recommendations contained i n para 33 of the 1 
st  Report of the 
Committee, all the Orders including rules etc., are  required to be laid on the Table of 
the House: - 
(a)  within a period of 15 days after their publica tion in the Gazette, if the 
House is in session; and 
(b)  if the House is not in session, within a perio d of 15 days after the 
commencement  of  the  next  session. 
-2- 

            However, in case of notifications relat ing to a state under the President’s rule, 
due to difficulties faced by certain Ministry, the Committee vide its recommendations 
contained in its 6 th  Report (para 17-19) relaxed this time period to 30  days from the 
date of publication of the rules, orders, notifications etc., in the State Gazette. 
 1.5       Motion for annulment or modification of r ules/regulations laid on the 
Table of the House  
             As per recommendations of the Committe e contained in its 10 th  Report ( cited 
at para 1.3 ante ), after the rules/regulations are laid on the Tabl e of the House, 
Members can move motion for modification or annulme nt of the rules/regulations. 
The statutory period of laying of 30 days might be completed in one session or two or 
more successive sessions. Further, as per the recom mendation of the Committee 
contained in its 75 th  Report (Para 2.5), reproduced below:- 
  
"The Committee agrees with the view of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation 
Lok Sabha (Seventh Lok Sabha) expressed in its 20 th  Report, that laying on the 
Table of all Orders' in pursuance of powers delegat ed by Parliament is very 
significant, as it affords an opportunity to Member s of Parliament if they so desire 
to move any amendment or modification to such 'orde r'; including a Motion for 
their annulment.”  
            Hence, a reading of both these recommen dations together indicates that 
Members have a right to suggest/move motion for ann ulment/modifications in the 
'Order' for a time period till one additional sessi on immediately following the session 
in which the period of 30 days is completed. If the  modification or annulment is 
carried by the Houses of Parliament, the rules/regu lations stand annulled or modified 
to the extent agreed to by the Houses of Parliament. 
 1.6       Role of the Committee on Subordinate Legi slation, Rajya Sabha with 
regard to unjustifiable delay in laying  
  
            One of the important functions of the C ommittee, according to Rule 209 (viii), 
is to see whether there has been unjustifiable dela y in the publication or laying of the 
rules/regulations before the Parliament. The Commit tee monitors the laying of the 
rules/regulations etc. on the Table of Rajya Sabha during its Session through its 
Reports. This practice started with the 131 
st  Report of the Committee on Statutory 
Orders laid on the Table of the Rajya Sabha during its 190 th  Session, presented to the 
House on 15 th  December, 2000. During the meeting of the Committe e held on 11 th  
December, 2000, to adopt the said report, the Commi ttee decided that henceforth, it 
will regularly scrutinize  the  notifications laid  on  the Table  of  Rajya Sabha from 
-3- 

time to time and present a report to the Council in  respect of each Session. This 
practice has continued since then and the present r eport is in pursuance of the said 
decision of the Committee.

              RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS  
           At the outset the Committee would like t o commend the 
Ministries/Departments of the Government of India for the marked improvement 
in the timely laying of notifications on the Table of  Rajya Sabha by them. The 
Committee notes and appreciates that this Parliamen tary Session is the first one, 
after the Nation-wide lockdown due to covid-19 was lifted, and  hardships  faced 
by all officials due to the disruption of their dut ies. However, despite this, the 
Ministries/Departments managed to lay 291 Gazette N otifications on the Table of 
Rajya Sabha, during the short duration of its 252 nd  Session of  Rajya Sabha. 
Further, out of these, only 15 Notifications were d elayed and 5 of them were 
delayed by a period of more than 10 months.  
            The Committee observes that 5 Notificat ions, which account for 33.3% of 
all the delayed Notifications were late by more tha n 10 months; 2 Notifications, 
which come to 13.33% of all the delayed Notificatio ns, were late by 9 months; 6 
Notifications, which come to 40% of all the delayed  Notifications were late by 8 
months; and 2 Notifications, which come to 13.33% o f all the delayed 
Notifications, were late by 7 months. This shows th at most of the 
Ministries/Departments have put in a good effort to obviate delay in placing these 
Notifications  on  the Table of Rajya Sabha. The only issue  was  that barring one  
-9- 

Ministry,  i.e. Ministry of Corporate Affairs, none  of the other 
Ministries/Departments has made any sincere effort to identify the logical 
reasons for the delay in laying and no delay statem ent was attached to the rest of 
the delayed Notifications.  
            The Committee observes that  some of th e Ministries, which had multiple 
delayed Notifications, e.g., Ministries of Commerce  and Industry (Department of 
Commerce); Consumer  Affairs, Food and Public Distr ibution (Department of 
Food and Public Distribution); and Corporate Affair s, they all need to review 
their procedure followed for laying of their Gazett e Notifications and if 
necessary,  issue instructions to all their Departments and sub ordinate/attached 
offices/organizations, impressing upon them the imp ortance of laying all 
notifications within the stipulated time and if the re is any delay, then to attach a 
delay statement, explaining cogent reasons for the delay and to take steps to 
obviate such delays in future. The Committee, after  considering the above data, 
makes the following recommendations and directs tha t these  recommendations 
may be circulated to all the Ministries/Departments  for strict compliance. The 
Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs may take necessar y step to co-ordinate with 
other Ministries/Departments on this serious issue. 
4.         RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE  
 a) Delay in Laying of Orders/Rules/Regulations  
     
4.1    The Committee notes that out of 15 delayed notif ications laid by the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India, duri ng the 252 nd  Session of 
Rajya Sabha, 2 Notifications were delayed by 7 mont hs; 6 Notifications were 
delayed by 8 months; 2 Notifications by 9 months; a nd 5 Notifications by 10 or 
more months. The Committee would like to draw the a ttention of few Ministries 
whose Notifications were laid on the Table of Rajya  Sabha after a considerable 
delay e.g., Commerce and Industry (Department of Co mmerce) - 1 year; 
Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution (Department of Food and Public 
Distribution) - 1 year and 1 month; and 1 year and 5 months. The Committee, 
once again, impresses upon all Ministries/Departments in general and specifically 
those mentioned above, to avoid such delays in the future. The Committee feels 
that such delays are totally avoidable and in viola tion of its recommendations 
contained in its 131 st  Report wherein it had recommended:- 
         
        “Orders required to be laid before the Hous e should be laid (i) if the House 
is not in Session, during the Session immediately following the date of publication 
of the Order in the Official Gazette and (ii) if th e House is in Session, on the date 
of the publication of the Order, during its continu ance and in case the time lag 
between the date of publication and the date of the  closing of the Session is less 
than 15 clear days, before the expiry of the Sessio n immediately following the 
said Session. All the Ministries/Departments of Gov ernment of India should 

henceforth comply with this schedule in the matter of laying of the Orders issued 
under various Acts of Parliament on the Table of the Rajya Sabha.”  
            The Committee, while reiterating its ab ove recommendations, once again 
recommends that the Ministries of Commerce and Indu stry (Department of 
Commerce); Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distri bution (Department of 
Food and Public Distribution); Corporate Affairs; a nd Finance (Department of 
Economic Affairs), (Department of Financial Service s) and (Department of 
Revenue) should ensure that all its notifications a re laid on the Table of Rajya 
Sabha within the prescribed time of 15 days.  
 b) Non-attachment of ‘Delay Statements’ to the delayed Notifications laid  
 4.2        The Committee feels that the most disconcert ing point is that only 1 
Notification out of a total 15 delayed Notification s that were laid during this 
Session, had delay statement appended to it, which is the only flaw in the 
performance of the Ministries/Departments during th e entire 252 nd  Session. The 
Committee would, therefore,  urge the Ministries/De partments to address this 
issue and ensure that in case, the delay in laying of Notifications is unavoidable, 
the Ministry should attach a delay statement from t heir Minister citing cogent 
reasons for the delay. The Committee had, in its ea rlier Report (135th Report) 
recommended that:- 
        “The Committee has, time and again, emphasi zed that it is essential that in 
case there is a delay in the laying of Statutory Or ders, the concerned 
Ministry/Department should invariably append a dela y statement along with the 
Notifications being laid so as to apprise the Parliament of the causes of delay. The 
Committee desires all Ministries/Departments to tak e a note of this, since the 
intention is that through the process of formulatio n of a delay statement, the 
Ministry is able to introspect, identify bottleneck s and devise remedial 
measures”.  
             The Committee recommends that all the Ministries/Departments must 
adhere to the time schedule for laying of Notificat ions as prescribed in 
Committee’s 131 st  Report and append a delay statement in case there is  delay in 
laying. The delay statement gives an opportunity, t o the Ministry to clarify the 
reasons for the delay in laying of the Notification . In case this longstanding 
recommendation of the Committee is not followed, th en the accountability of the 
Ministries to the Parliament and the Constitutional Mandate of the Parliament to 
monitor the functioning of the Executive would beco me a futile exercise and the 
Committee has every right to take this matter very seriously.  
-11- 
  

c) Format of Delay Statements  
 4.3    The Committee further observes that none of the Ministries/Departments, 
whose Notifications were delayed, has made any sinc ere efforts to identify the 
reasons for the delay in laying them. The Committee , therefore, strongly 
recommends that the Ministries/Departments should c ite cogent, logical and self 
explanatory reasons for the delay in the laying of Notifications so that 
accountability of the Ministries/Departments to the  Parliament is maintained  in 
its true letter and spirit and to ensure that, it d oes remain a mere formality. In 
this connection, Committee would like to re-iterate  its recommendations 
contained in para 2(xii) of its 189 th  Report, which is reproduced below:- 
              “The Committee is not happy at the ca sual manner in which the 
Ministries have treated its recommendations with re gard to the delay in the 
laying of the Notifications despite the Committee’s  reiteration in all its reports. 
The Committee takes serious note of the fact that, in most cases, the Ministries 
fail to append delay statements explaining the reas ons for the delay. Therefore, 
the Committee reiterates, that the Ministries shoul d take proactive measures so 
as to avoid any delay, whatsoever, in the laying of  the Notifications and that the 
Committee is unable to accept the flimsy grounds gi ven by the Ministries 
regarding the reasons for delay.”  
       The Committee, therefore, recommends these M inistries/Departments to 
not only ensure timely laying of Notifications but also follow the practice of 
enclosing a delay statement in case(s) of delays.  
 d) EARLIER IMPORTANT RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
ON SUBORDINATE  LEGISLATION, RAJYA SABHA  
 4.4       The Committee in its earlier recommendations, for strict compliance by all the 
Ministries/Departments of the Government of India, had stated that:- 
  
Formula for laying of Statutory Rules 
 
            The Committee approve the following draft revised f ormula for laying of 
Statutory Rules before both Houses of Parliament which the Ministry of Law and 
Justice propose to incorporate in all future legisl ation which provide for making 
of rules by the Central Government:— 
  
        "Every rule made by the Central Government under this Act shall be 
laid, as soon as may be after it is made, before ea ch House of Parliament, 
while it is in session, for a total period of thirt y days which may be 
comprised in one session or in two or more successi ve sessions, and if, before 
the expiry of the session immediately following the  session or the successive 
sessions aforesaid, both Houses agree in making any modification in the  rule  
or  both   Houses  agree  that the  rule  should not  be  made,  the  rule  shall  
-12 - 

thereafter have effect only in such modified form o r be of no effect, as the 
case may be; so, however that any such modification  or annulment shall be 
without prejudice to the validity of anything previ ously done under that 
rule."  
             
            The Committee recommends that the revis ed formula should be 
incorporated not only in new legislation but also i n the existing Acts as and when 
Bills to amend them are brought before Parliament. The Ministry should also 
incorporate the new formula in the Bills pending be fore Parliament. This will, in 
the opinion of the Committee, bring about uniformity in the matter expeditiously.  
(10 
th  Report)  
(Presented on 24 th  May, 1971)  
 Incorporating corrections and amendments in the order  
             “The Committee desires that for the con venience of the public and 
Members, Ministries should henceforth send copies o f 'order' duly authenticated 
by the Ministers concerned, incorporating therein a ll the corrections and 
amendments issued till date of laying such 'orders'  instead of laying the 
uncorrected copy along with corrigenda. The Committ ee feels that to obviate any 
legal or technical difficulty, Ministries should ex amine whether there is any 
necessity of assigning a separate G.S.R. No. to a c orrigendum at the time of its 
publication in the Gazette and whether such a corri gendum should not be 
published without assigning any G.S.R. No. The Committee would, therefore, like 
to impress upon all Ministries of the Government of  India that the present 
practice of laying the rules without incorporating corrigenda in the body of the 
rules is not a healthy one. The Committee hopes tha t the Ministries will ensure 
supply of only corrected copies of the rules for la ying on the Table so that they 
depict a true and correct picture and serve the desired purpose."  
            (7 th  Report)  
(Presented on 12 th  May, 1969)  
 Assigning distinctive number to each Notification  
        “In the opinion of the Committee, every not ification should be assigned a 
distinctive number in order to give it a separate i dentity and similarly, no 
notification should be published/laid which does no t carry a notification number. 
The Committee expects all Ministries/Departments of  Government of India to 
exercise caution in this regard. In case where ther e are more than one 
Notifications  under a single file, the  Ministries/Departments should  ensure that 
-13 - 

 the file number on each notification should be sui tably distinguished from one 
another.”  
(152 nd  Report)  
(Presented on 26 th  August, 2004)  
Time limit for rule making process  
  
“The Committee feels that the rule-making process c ould well have been 
completed within the time limit of six months which  the Committee has 
laid down for making of rules under an Act after co ming into force of 
that Act. ................. Where however, a Minist ry does not find it possible 
to adhere to the time limit, they should inform the  Committee of the 
reasons why they cannot make rules within the time limit and seek 
extension of time for completing the rule-making process.”  
(47 th   Report)  
(Presented on 14 th  September, 1981)  
             “In addition to the concern expressed by the Committee over delay in 
laying of Notifications on the Table of the House, the Committee also express 
their deep concern over delay in framing of rules/r egulations under different 
Acts. The Committee in its 47 th  report presented to the House on 14.9.1981 has 
recommended that the rule-making process should be completed within a period 
of six months of the coming into force of an Act. T he Committee has further 
recommended that in case a Ministry is not able to adhere to this time limit, it 
should seek extension of time for completing the ru le-making process. The 
recommendation of the committee reads as follows:- 
               “The Committee feels that the rule-making process could well have been 
completed within the time limit of six months which the Committee has laid down 
for making of rules under an Act after coming into force of that Act. Where 
however, a Ministry does not find it possible to ad here to the time limit, they 
should inform the Committee of the reasons why they  cannot make rules within 
the time limit and seek extension of time for compl eting the rule-making 
process.”  
            The Committee is constrained to take no te of the fact that the 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India are n ot complying with the 
Committee’s recommendation to complete the process of framing of subordinate 
legislation contemplated under various Acts of Parl iament within a period of six 
months. At the same time, the Committee also does n ot receive requests for 
extension of time for completing the rule-making pr ocess in terms of its 
recommendations as above from most of the Ministrie s/Departments. The 
Committee takes a serious note of the prevailing si tuation in which the 
Ministries/Departments  are  neither  able to  complete   the  task  of  framing 
-14- 

 rules/regulations under different Acts within the given six months’ period nor do 
they suo-motu  approach the Committee for seeking extension of ti me. The 
Committee further notes that in order to ensure tim ely framing of 
rules/regulations it has taken an initiative to mon itor the progress of framing of 
subordinate legislation in respect of all legislati ons brought about by different 
Ministries/Departments of Government of India from the year 2003 onwards 
with a view to ensure that the framing of subordina te legislation is not delayed. 
The Committee, however, finds that the responses fr om the 
Ministries/Departments have not been prompt in this  monitoring exercise 
undertaken on behalf of the Committee. 
  
            In view of the above position, the Comm ittee once again reiterates its 
recommendation that the Ministries/Departments shou ld ensure putting in place 
subordinate legislation positively within a period of six months of coming into 
force of the Act. The Committee further recommends that in case the Ministry 
fails to meet with this deadline, they should invar iably approach the Committee 
for seeking extension of time. The Committee furthe r recommends that in cases 
where the time limit of six months is not adhered t o, they should, while laying 
rules/regulations before the Parliament invariably lay a statement explaining the 
reasons why the framing of rules/regulations was de layed beyond six months so 
as to keep the Parliament apprised of the complianc e of the Parliament’s 
mandate  conferred upon the Executive.”  
(192 
nd  Report)  
(Presented on 26 th  August, 2011)  
  
The Committee observes that the whole process of en acting laws is 
defeated if rules are not framed and laid on the Ta ble of the House in time.  A 
reasonable delay could be understood but unjustifia bly long delays should be 
avoided and the Ministries should work towards impr oving this position.   The 
Committee hopes that Ministry would strive to keep the delay to the minimum 
and take care that Notifications are laid on the Ta ble of the House at the first 
available opportunity after publication of Notifications.  
  
The Committee would like to impress upon the Minist ry that it is their 
responsibility to ensure that copies of the Notific ations are printed timely and for 
this purpose, they need to evolve a suitable mechan ism to ensure that 
notifications are laid in time.   The Committee is happy that the Ministry has 
evolved an internal mechanism/ procedure for this p urpose.  The Committee 
hopes that it would take action accordingly in orde r to comply with the 
prescribed schedule in the matter of laying of statutory Notifications.

The Ministry must take appropriate step to remove l acuna, if any, 
administrative or otherwise, causing such long dela y by being little proactive and 
prompt.  Further, the Ministries should take it up with the Ministry of Urban 
Development for late receiving of printed copies of the Notification.  
212 th  Report  
(Presented on 3 rd  September, 2013)  
  
Planning to lay papers during the initial stages of the Session  
         "The Committee recommends that Ministries should pl an to lay their 
papers during the initial/middle stages of the sess ion rather than scheduling this 
work towards the close of the session in order to avoid such happenings."  
173 rd   Report  
(Presented on 22 nd  April, 2008)  
  
Uploading Notifications on websites 
 
             Rules/Regulations/Orders/bye-laws are laid by different Ministries on the 
Table of the House under various provisions of pare nt Acts passed by 
Parliament. These Rules/ Regulations/Orders/bye-law s are published in the 
official Gazette before being laid on the Table of the House. Even after they are 
laid, it is very difficult to get access to these N otifications. The Committee 
recommends that such Rules/Regulations/Orders, etc.  laid on the Table of the 
House should be invariably uploaded on the websites  of respective Ministries 
immediately on the same day when they have been laid on the Table of the House, 
for information of Members of Parliament and people  at large for their easy 
access.  
  
201 st  Report  
(Presented on 14 th  December, 2012)  
 Late availability of printed copies  
             “The Committee is not inclined to accep t the late availability of printed 
copies of Notifications from the Government of Indi a Press as the reason for 
delay in laying of the Notifications. The Committee  directs all the Ministries that 
in  case  there  is  a  delay  in  procuring printed copies  in time,  they  may  obtain

G.S.R. and S.O. numbers from the Government of Indi a Press and prepare 
requisite number of copies in cyclostyled form for laying in the Parliament. The 
Committee also recommends that this process may be adopted by Ministries suo 
moto  on immediate basis so as to avoid such delays henceforth”. 
213 th  Report
