2. In his Opening remarks, one of the Members of the Committee welcomed the Officers
from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, FSSAI, and other participants, appreciating
their commitment to public health and consumer welfare. He emphasized the importance and
timeliness of the discussion on the Food Safety and Standards (Labelling and Display)

26


Regulations, 2020, highlighting their impact on nutritional awareness, product authenticity,
and consumer empowerment. Acknowledging the efforts made by the Ministry and FSSAI, it
was stressed that there is need to consider stakeholder input, assess industry readiness, and
align regulations with global best practices and for these the Committee has decided to
examine these Regulations.

3. Following this, in his presentation, CEO FSSAI presented a comprehensive overview
of food labelling regulations in India, tracing their evolution from the Agricultural Produce
(Grading and Marking) Act of 1937 (AGMARK) to the Food Safety and Standards Authority
of India (FSSAI) Regulations of 2020. He mentioned that initially, labeling was optional
under acts like AGMARK and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act (PFA) of 1954,
which introduced mandatory labeling requirements such as product name, ingredients, net
weight, and prohibitions on false claims. Subsequent legislation, including the Infant Milk
Substitutes Act of 1992 and the Legal Metrology Act of 2009, further refined labelling
provisions, addressing specific products like genetically modified foods and infant milk
substitutes. The Food Safety and Standards Act (FSSA) of 2006 consolidated these efforts,
leading to the comprehensive Packaging and Labelling Regulations of 2011, which were later
bifurcated into separate regulations for packaging, labelling, and advertising in 2018 and
2020.

4. He stated that the Food Safety & Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020
introduced significant updates, mandating nutritional information based on Recommended
Dietary Allowance (RDA) per 100 grams, allergen declarations, and specific logos for
fortified, vegan, and Ayurvedic foods. Also Front-of-pack labeling became mandatory for
multi-source edible oils, pan masala warnings, and vegetarian/non-vegetarian declarations.
Amendments in 2021 and 2022 reduced label size requirements, exempted certain products
from allergen declarations, and standardized labelling for breads like whole wheat and
multigrain. It was submitted that the regulations align with global standards like the Codex
Alimentarius and include India-specific requirements, such as vegan and Ayurvedic logos. It
was informed that E-commerce and food service establishments with over 10 outlets must
also comply with labelling requirements, including calorific value disclosures.

5. CEO, FSSAI submitted that enforcement of the Regulations is robust, with penalties
under the FSSA ranging from Rs. 5-10 lakhs for civil offences like misbranding to
imprisonment for criminal violations causing injury or death. It was informed that in 2023-
24, over 4 lakh food samples were tested, identifying 33,000 non-conforming cases, with
29,000 penalties imposed. Also, the Advertisement Monitoring Committee addressed 577
misleading claims, closing 280 cases after corrections. He further informed that a draft Front-
of-Pack Nutrition Labelling (FOPNL) regulation, notified in 2022, proposes a star-rating
system (0.5 to 5 stars) based on positive and negative nutrients, harmonized with
international practices and over 14,000 stakeholder comments are under review, with ongoing
consultations to finalize amendments, reflecting a scientific and inclusive approach to
improving food labelling standards in India.

27


6. The Chairman emphasized the need for FSSAI to align with the Prime Minister’s
anti-obesity campaign, citing Singapore’s simple A-D nutri-code as a model for clear,
consumer-friendly labelling to combat obesity. He urged FSSAI to enhance its institutional
capacity and update regulations in response to a Supreme Court directive to finalize Front-of-
Pack Nutrition Labelling (FOPNL) within three months. He also sought information on the
coordination between FSSAI and the Ministry of Consumer Affairs on misleading
advertisements. CEO, FSSAI acknowledged the Supreme Court’s directive on FOPNL,
noting that a 2022 draft notification received over 14,000 stakeholder comments, and an
Expert Committee is reviewing them. He confirmed FSSAI’s commitment to stakeholder
consultations for adopting a simpler nutri-code like Singapore’s A-D system. On misleading
advertisements, he clarified that FSSAI regulates food-related claims, issuing show-cause
notices and penalties while coordinating with the Consumer Affairs Ministry for broader
issues. He also clarified that alcohol falls under FSSAI’s labelling purview, with warning
sizes increased to 50% of the label. For ice cream, he noted that vegetable oil-based frozen
desserts are permitted but must be clearly labelled as non-milk products, similar to paneer
analogues and vanaspati.

7. During the meeting, Members raised a range of critical queries and concerns regarding
the implementation and effectiveness of food labelling regulations. Concerns were voiced
about the unclear display of manufacturing and expiry dates on food products, with
suggestions to prevent companies from manipulating dates to boost sales, FSSAI’s approach
to updating the National Health Rating in line with evolving WHO guidelines, and how it
balances input from medical experts and industry stakeholders and the mechanism for
random post-market inspections and jurisdiction over counterfeit products like fake rice and
milk powder. Challenges in the grassroots implementation of labelling rules, particularly
confusion around drinking water safety and hotel food adulteration and the scientific basis for
star ratings were also mentioned.

8. In response to the Members' queries, CEO, FSSAI informed the measures taken by
FSSAI to address various concerns submitting that on the issue of illegibly small expiry
dates, major manufacturers already withdraw products well before expiration, FSSAI engages
smaller producers through platforms like FICCI and state-level meetings to enforce similar
practices. On the Health Star Rating system, it was submitted that it is based on ICMR and
National Institute of Nutrition guidelines, with inputs from international data and stakeholder
consultations aimed at balancing public health and industry views. Regarding enforcement, it
was mentioned that each food safety officer is mandated to conduct 25 sample checks
monthly, with over four lakh samples tested in 2023-24 across 247 labs, and all data is being
uploaded to the INFoLNET portal. He also highlighted awareness initiatives including Eat
Right Melas, Eat Right Schools, and certified campuses. Addressing online labelling
exemptions, he clarified that these apply only to e-commerce listings, not physical products,
which must comply fully. It was also informed that labeling is permitted in English, Hindi, or
regional languages and underlined the agency’s guidelines promoting healthy diets in
schools, including bans on high-fat/salt/sugar foods.

9. The Chairman of the Committee mentioned that in future meetings, submissions of
ICMR, WHO India, and nutrition experts and industry associations besides stakeholder
Ministries shall also be taken.

At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members and the officials present. He stated
that this was the third meeting of the Committee during its examination of The Food Safety
and Standards (Labelling and Display) Regulations, 2020 and the subsequent amendments.
The Committee had earlier held two meetings on 2nd May and 18" June, 2025, during
which it heard the Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare; the CEO, Food
Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI); and representatives of the National
Institute of Nutrition (NIN).

2. The Chairman noted that the Committee has been exploring various aspects of
front-of-pack labelling and measures to promote healthier food choices. He recalled that
the Committee had decided in its previous meeting to seek the views of the Ministry of
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) and representatives from the food
industry, as many food sellers belong to the unorganised sector represented by the MSME
Ministry. The Secretary, Ministry of MSME, was then invited to make a brief submission.
3. The Secretary, Ministry of MSME, made a presentation outlining the definition,
role, and contribution of MSMEs to economic growth, particularly in the food processing
sector. He also highlighted challenges faced by MSMEs, such as financial constraints and
procedural complexities, and suggested ways to facilitate better implementation of the
Labelling and Display Regulations, 2020. He emphasized that the Ministry serves as the
nodal agency for MSMEs, dealing with size-based classifications and normative aspects.
The Secretary reiterated that MSMEs are key engines of economic growth, contributing
significantly to GDP, exports, employment, empowerment, and environmental
sustainability.

4. The Secretary informed the Committee that the Government is actively exploring
mechanisms to simplify compliance frameworks and reduce the compliance burden without
compromising basic standards. He suggested that FSSAI could adopt a more scale-sensitive
and capacity-based approach in this regard. He further proposed that, similar to income tax
and GST thresholds, FSSAI could consider introducing threshold-based licensing
requirements, grounded in sound empirical and public health criteria.

5. Highlighting the need for strengthening common infrastructure—such as cold
chains, testing laboratories, and packaging units—the Secretary underlined that access to
affordable credit remains critical for MSME capacity building. He also noted that digital on
boarding for MSMEs onto e-marketplaces could enhance their competitiveness while
naturally improving standards of hygiene, packaging, and marketing. On research and
development, he observed that small industries lack resources to undertake R&D
independently, and suggested that targeted support mechanisms be developed to promote
innovation and quality enhancement in the MSME food sector. The Secretary stressed the
importance of capacity enhancement and State Government participation, as industry is a
State subject. He recommended that stakeholder consultations by regulatory bodies such as
BIS, FSSAI, and QCI be made more inclusive, sector-specific, and grounded in the
realities of MSMEs.

6. The Chairman and Members raised queries regarding expiry and use-by dates
under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, the FSS Act, and issues relating to the cold
chain. The officials present responded to these queries.

36


7. The Committee then interacted with representatives of the food industry.
Welcoming them, the Chairman highlighted the Hon’ble Prime Minister’s vision of an
obesity-free India and the need to encourage healthier consumer choices. He expressed
concern over increasing trends of obesity and sought the industry’s perspective on the
proposed labelling regulations and their implications.

8. The representative of CIFTI informed the Committee that CIFTI facilitates the
food sector by addressing quality concerns and interpreting food laws. He clarified the
distinction between “expiry” and “best before” dates, suggesting that “expiry/use by”
should be mandatory only for perishable and high-risk foods, while “best before” should
apply to others. He recommended a holistic review of Schedule II to remove redundant
declarations, the use of QR codes to reduce label clutter, and as cience-based revision of
definitions related to “unsafe food.”

9. The representative of the Indian Dairy Association (IDA) stated that while the
current regulations suit the dairy industry, the proposed star-rating system could cause
consumer confusion. He noted anomalies in the algorithm, where nutritious products like
paneer received the same or lower ratings than less healthy items. IDA suggested expert
review of the algorithm, default five-star ratings for natural dairy products, and exemption
of natural saturated fats and sodium from negative highlighting.

10. The All-India Food Processors’ Association (AIFPA) expressed concern that the
proposed star-rating system could harm traditional food industries, confuse consumers, and
negatively affect farmers and the economy. They argued that such a system could reinforce
misconceptions about processed foods and damage India’s traditional food heritage.

11. The Indian Food & Beverage Association (IFBA) recommended that front-of-pack
labelling focus on providing balanced nutritional information to help consumers make
informed choices. They emphasised the importance of robust enforcement, consumer
education, and policy integration, and called for harmonisation across different regulatory
authorities to establish a “One Nation, One Law” framework.

12. The Forum of Indian Food Importers (FIFI) opposed the star- rating system,
stating that it fails to capture the nutritional value of products comprehensively. They also
recommended that annual labeling changes coincide with the start of the financial year (1st
April) rather than July, to align with business cycles and allow adequate time for
compliance.

13. Members of the Committee raised further queries, which were duly responded to
by the representatives of the food industry. Chairman of the Committee also asked the food
industry representatives present to submit any further submissions that they may have on
these Rules for consideration.

14. A verbatim record of the proceedings was maintained.

15. The meeting adjourned at 4.18 p.m.
